title: How to Stop the Scroll: 36 Hooks for Short-Form Videos
markdown:
# How to Stop the Scroll: 36 Hooks for Short-Form Videos

At 0:02, the thumb moves. Your video may be clear, well shot, and useful—but the opening gave someone no reason to stay.

![Three Hook Lab hooks for one video](https://uploads.postiz.com/8cLEoX1RU8.png)

This page gives you 36 ready-to-adapt opening lines for the moment before the swipe, plus a simple way to choose and test one. Replace the bracketed details with your real subject, result, or constraint.

## Problem-first hooks

Use these when the viewer already feels the problem and wants a fast explanation.

1. “If [problem] keeps happening, check this before you change anything.”
2. “The reason [desired result] still feels hard is probably not what you think.”
3. “You are not bad at [activity]. You may be starting at the wrong step.”
4. “Before you spend another [time/money], fix this part of [topic].”
5. “This is why your [thing] looks good but still does not work.”
6. “If you only have [ADD: your time], do this part first.”

## Contrarian hooks

Use these when you can challenge a familiar piece of advice, then explain the condition that makes your view true.

7. “Stop trying to [common advice] if your goal is [specific outcome].”
8. “You do not need more [tool/effort]. You need a better first move.”
9. “The popular way to [task] is making this harder.”
10. “Do less of [habit] before you add another strategy.”
11. “The fastest way to improve [outcome] may be to remove this step.”
12. “Everyone tells beginners to [advice]. I would start here instead.”

## Mistake hooks

Use these when the audience can recognize itself in a common, specific error.

13. “This small [topic] mistake costs you [specific consequence].”
14. “You are probably doing [task] in the right order for the wrong result.”
15. “The first [number] seconds of your [video/process] are losing people here.”
16. “Do not make this beginner mistake with [topic].”
17. “If [result] is not happening, this is the mistake I would check first.”
18. “Your [thing] is not failing because it is boring. It is failing because of this.”

## Question hooks

Use a question only when the answer creates a tension the viewer wants resolved.

19. “Why does [problem] happen after you do everything right?”
20. “What would change if you stopped [habit] for [ADD: duration]?”
21. “Why do people quit [activity] right when it starts to work?”
22. “Can you get [result] without [common sacrifice]?”
23. “What is the one thing beginners miss about [topic]?”
24. “Why does this simple [object/action] make such a difference?”

## Demonstration hooks

Use these when the proof can be shown immediately on screen.

25. “Watch what changes when I move this one step earlier.”
26. “Here is [topic] before and after one adjustment.”
27. “I am going to fix this [item] in [ADD: duration].”
28. “This is the difference between [version A] and [version B].”
29. “Pause here if your [thing] looks like this.”
30. “I tested two ways to [task]. This is the one I would keep.”

## Specific-result hooks

Use these when you have a real, supportable result or a sharply defined outcome. Do not replace the blank with a made-up number.

31. “How I got [real result] from [specific action].”
32. “The [number]-step way to make [task] less overwhelming.”
33. “I changed [one variable] and got [real observed result].”
34. “A [ADD: duration] reset for when [specific problem] hits.”
35. “The exact checklist I use before I [task].”
36. “From [starting state] to [desired state]: the first thing to change.”

## Pick the hook that matches the video

Start with the viewer’s immediate reason for stopping. If they already know the pain, use a problem or mistake hook. If they think they know the answer, use a contrarian hook. If the visual is compelling by itself, lead with a demonstration. If your video gives a process, make the promised outcome specific.

A hook is a promise, not the whole video. The next sentence must pay off the opening line: name the mistake, show the comparison, or begin the first step. If the opening asks a question, answer it quickly enough that the question does not become bait.

## Test without guessing

Make two or three opening versions for the same video. Keep the subject, footage, and main lesson consistent; change only the first spoken line and matching on-screen text. Then watch the opening back with the sound off, then with your eyes on the captions. Can a new viewer tell what is at stake before the first beat ends?

Choose the version that is most precise about the viewer, problem, and payoff. “A better morning routine” is broad. “What to do when your morning plan falls apart by 8:30” gives a person a situation they can recognize.

## FAQ

### Should every hook be dramatic?

No. A clear promise can beat a dramatic one. Match the energy to the subject and audience; urgency works best when the video can deliver it.

### Should the spoken line and on-screen text be identical?

They can be, but they do not have to be. Let the spoken line carry the idea while the text gives the viewer a fast, readable anchor.

### How long should the hook be?

Make it as short as the idea allows. The goal is to establish a reason to continue before the viewer swipes, then move into proof, context, or the first useful step.

### What if none of these lines sound like me?

Keep the underlying structure and rewrite the wording in your natural voice. Specificity matters more than copying a phrase exactly.

## What the tool returns

Here is a published example of the format you receive:

**You send:** "Hooks for a 30s TikTok about why most people quit the gym in January — energetic, for beginners."

**You get back (shortened):**
- **Positioning:** "The gym isn't the problem — your first week is." You own the beginner-who-keeps-quitting angle.
- **Hooks (5+, each with spoken line + on-screen text + type):**
  1. *Contrarian* — 🗣 "Stop going to the gym every day." / 🖥 "Day 1 is where you quit"
  2. *Question* — 🗣 "Why does everyone quit by January 20th?" / 🖥 "The January 20th wall"
  3. *Mistake* — 🗣 "You're not lazy. You're doing week one wrong." / 🖥 "Week 1 mistake"
- **Recommended pick:** #3, with one line on why it fits a beginner audience.
- **Script:** 0–3s hook · 3–10s the mistake · 10–22s the fix in 3 steps · 22–30s CTA.
- **Caption:** short caption + CTA + hashtags, plus one filming tip.

Turn one topic into hook options, a recommended direction, and a short script with [Hook Lab](https://capafy.ai/agent/8123079349?ct=hooklab_blog).
